subject: Question about sample level density estimates

messages.author: 45906a28df896f54
messages.subject: Question about sample level density estimates
parts:
Hi Everyone,

I'm currently trying to generate sample-level density estimates from a set of point counts where each point was visited 3 times, each time by a different observer. I've gone though the model selection process and have settled on one model (MCDS with hazard rate key, simple polynomial adjustment, and observer as a covariate) that by all measures seems to be the best model and has good fit. However, when I go to generate sample-level density estimates for this model, my resulting density/abundance estimates seem to be occurring at discrete intervals (i.e. 9, 18, 27, etc) rather than along a continuous range.

I found an older posting asking essentially the same question here:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/distance-sampling/sample$20level$20density%7Csort:relevance/distance-sampling/2XA2SkjT2ak/xYAYKqStp5IJ

Based on the recommendations from this posting I've made sure that my model specifies only "sample" for the level of resolution for the density estimate, and that both "sample" and "global" are checked for the detection function, however my resulting density estimates are still occurring in discrete intervals. As a comparison I've tried generating point-specific density estimates from other models (both CDS and MCDS) and still get density estimates occurring only in intervals.

Am I still doing something wrong in trying to estimate point-specific densities, and if not can anyone explain why I'm not getting a continuous range of density estimates?


Thanks,
Nathaniel Behl



M.S. student, Benkman Lab
Department of Zoology & Physiology
University of Wyoming

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Question about sample level density estimates
parts:
Nathaniel

Sorry I didn't answer this when you originally posted the question in mid-January.

The explanation for the abundance estimates you observed has to do with the nature of transect-level estimate.  Estimates for each of your points is simply the number of detections at that point scaled up by dividing count by probability of detection.

The example you so helpfully provided "my abundance estimates seem to be occurring at discrete intervals (i.e. 9, 18, 27, etc)" made it easy to deduce that via your fitted detection function, the estimated probability of detecting a bird (given it is within the truncation distance of the point) was 0.11.

Therefore, at points where there was a single detection, the estimate of abundance is 9 (1/0.11); points were there were two detections had an estimated abundance of 18 (2/0.11), etc.  Because you have observer as a covariate, the divisor would differ for points sampled by different observers.

Producing estimates at the scale of the point transect washes out replication that would produce a more continuous range of estimates.

parts:
Hi Nathaniel, listfolk,

I wonder if you've thought about applying density surface modelling to
this problem (if you have the locations of your points and some useful
geographically-referenced data)?

Our paper from 2013 gives an outline of this approach
(http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12105/abstract).
As of a couple of dsm versions ago, you can perform this analysis for
point transects in R (not in Distance for Windows at the moment). There
are examples of line transect analyses on the distance website
(http://distancesampling.org/R/). One needs to specify that you're using
point transect data (transect="point") when running your model, not
currently featured in any examples on the website (though I am working
on that).

Hope this helps.

cheers,
--dave

Carolin

This may get you a part of your answer.

Given that your data structure is such that you have transects within strata (indicated via sample.label and region.label variables), ds() has likely produced the point estimates you desire.

I use the "tee data" provided and used in the example for the ds() function:

library(Distance)
data(book.tee.data)
tee.data<-book.tee.data$book.tee.dataframe[book.tee.data$book.tee.dataframe$observer==1,]
region <- book.tee.data$book.tee.region
samples <- book.tee.data$book.tee.samples
obs <- book.tee.data$book.tee.obs
ds.dht.model <- ds(tee.data,4,region.table=region,
                   sample.table=samples,obs.table=obs)
str(ds.dht.model$dht$individuals$bysample)

you will find that the object created by ds() (when region, sample and observation tables are provide) contains sample-specific point estimates of density and abundance.

Your challenge would be to produce measures of precision for those estimates; using the delta method.

I haven't closely read the paper by Acevedo et al. to know if they produced the figure you show at the sample-level or region-level; the paper describes them as "site" estimates.

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Question about sample level density estimates
parts:
Carolin

No, I meant approximation of variance approach called the delta method.  The calculation of the transect-level estimate is described in the function dht() as a Horvitz-Thompson-like estimator using estimated values of detection probability for each detection to scale-up the count to an estimate of abundance.

"Abundance is estimated with a Horvitz-Thompson-like estimator (Huggins 1989, 1991; Borchers et al 1998; Borchers and Burnham 2004). The abundance in the sampled region is simply 1/p_1 + 1/p_2 + ... + 1/p_nwhere p_i is the estimated detection probability for the ith detection of n total observations. It is not strictly a Horvitz-Thompson estimator because the p_i are estimated and not known. For animals observed in tight clusters, that estimator gives the abundance of groups (group=TRUE in options) and the abundance of individuals is estimated as s_1/p_1 + s_2/p_2 + ... + s_n/p_n, where s_i is the size (e.g., number of animals in the group) of each observation (group=FALSE in options)."

Calculation of precision for these point estimates should involve a) uncertainty in detection probability (derived from uncertainty in parameter estimates in your detection function -- that has several covariates as I recall) and b) uncertainty in the encounter rate.  However, your design has no uncertainty in encounter rate because you have no replicates at the sample level.  I suspect the software opts not to present a measure of precision based solely upon the uncertainty in the parameter estimates.  To my knowledge, those would be quite difficult calculations to carry out.

With regard to your second question of which of the cutpoint histograms to present.  Given a choice between the two you present, I would suggest you present the 20m cutpoints.  Keep in mind there is no requirement that the cutpoints be of equal width throughout the range of perpendicular distances.  With the 20m graph, you are better able to discuss the potential challenges in the data apparent in the first two bins.  This subtlety of the data is not apparent with the 30m histograms.
